segments.translation: Delighted, [Āryadeva]{p-aryadeva} sets out that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song with Āryadevapāda, delighted, setting out ‘that same meaning’ (cp.31.m1), presumably the meaning the preceding songs have set out. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has him ‘delighted by the meaning of reality’ instead.

flags.note: pramuditaṃ is accusative singular, so it agrees with arthaṃ (‘that same delighted meaning’), not with the honorific plural āryadevapādāḥ. It may be adverbial (‘joyfully’) or a slip for pramuditāḥ (‘delighted’). Either way the delight is Āryadeva’s, as in the Tibetan (rab tu dgyes pa'i 'phags pa lha). I translated ‘Delighted, Āryadeva…’.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads de kho na nyid kyi don gyis rab tu dgyes pa'i 'phags pa lha'i zhabs kyis gsungs te, ‘Āryadevapāda, delighted by the meaning of reality, said’. Its manuscript seems to have had tattvārtha- (‘the meaning of reality’) where the Nepal manuscript has tam evārthaṃ (‘that same meaning’); the two look alike. Munidatta opens other songs with tam evārthaṃ (glossary forms for Lūyī and Śānti), as here (cp.31.m1), so I kept the Sanskrit. The Tibetan also has ‘said’ (gsungs) for ‘sets out’ (pratipādayanti).

segments.translit: jahi maṇa ityādi| yasmin prabhāsvare saṃhāramaṇḍalādikrameṇa viṣayapavanendriyādikaṃ niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇaṃ| tatra praviṣṭe(ṣe) sati apā iti| cittarājasyoddeśaṃ na jānāmi kva gataḥ|
segments.translation: ‘Where [mind]{citta}…’ and so on. The [clear light]{prabhasvara} in which, by the sequence that begins with the [withdrawal]{upasamhara} of the [maṇḍala]{mandala}, [sense objects]{visaya}, [wind]{vayu}, [senses]{indriya} and the rest are made [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}: when all this has entered there, then ‘the [self]{atman}’: I do not know the whereabouts of the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, where it has gone.
segments.note: Munidatta takes ‘where’ as [clear light]{prabhasvara} (cp.31.m2). Sense objects, wind and senses, made without intrinsic nature by withdrawing the maṇḍala (the deity’s circle), enter it, and the poet cannot tell where the self, the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}, has gone. For 1a’s doubtful ho ṇa ṭhā his wording implies ‘made void’ and ‘entered there’; he does not quote the words.

flags.note: Bears on the song draft, 1a (ho ṇa ṭhā). Munidatta (cp.31.m2) does not quote these words. In their place his gloss says that sense objects, wind and senses ‘are made without intrinsic nature’ (niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇa) and ‘have entered there’ (tatra praviṣṭe), that is, into clear light. The first fits the draft’s ‘are lost’ (ṇaṭhā as naṣṭa). The second matches the Tibetan line, gang la yid dang dbang po rlung rnams zhugs gyur na, ‘where mind, senses and winds have entered’. If ṇa ṭhā is read as na sthā, ‘do not stay’, nothing in his gloss echoes it. He also lists sense objects where the song has mind, keeping the mind for the king of mind of 1b.

The first sentence has no finite verb: niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇaṃ is a verbal noun (‘the making without intrinsic nature’), which I turned into a passive clause. In praviṣṭe(ṣe) sati, Shastri’s (ṣe) points to praviṣṭeṣu (‘when they have entered’); but the singular praviṣṭe sati can agree with the collective neuter viṣayapavanendriyādikaṃ, so I translated ‘when all this has entered there’. The Tibetan (de la rab tu zhugs par gyur na) does not mark number.

saṃhāramaṇḍalādikrameṇa is literally ‘by the sequence of withdrawal–maṇḍala–and so on’. The Tibetan construes it as ‘by the sequence of withdrawing the maṇḍala and so on’ (dkyil 'khor la sogs pa sdud pa'i rim pas), and I followed it. A ‘maṇḍala of withdrawal’ is also possible.

Where the Sanskrit cites apā, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) cites bdag gis, ‘by me’, the agent of ‘do not know’, as in its line 1b (bdag gis mi shes). So it reads the word as the speaker, ‘I’, not as ‘the self’ that has gone. It renders uddeśa as mtshon pa, ‘pointing out’: ‘I do not know how to point out the king of mind, nor even where it has gone’.

segments.translit: dhruvapadena ānandaṃ dṛḍhayati— akaṭeti— āścaryaṃ| karuṇeti saṃvṛtibodhicittaṃ gurusampradāyāt| ḍamaruketi a(ma)nāhataśabdaṃ karoti| anāhataṃ hataṃ jñānaṃ vibudhyate| ataeva āryadevapādāḥ| nirālambena sarvadharmānupalambhayogena rājate śobhate|
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes [joy]{ananda} firm. ‘Akaṭa’: a [wonder]{adbhuta}. ‘[Compassion]{karuna}’: [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, by way of the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}. ‘[Ḍamaru]{damaru}’: it makes the [unstruck]{anahata} sound. [Unstruck]{anahata} [knowledge]{jnana} awakens. That is why [Āryadeva]{p-aryadeva} shines and is splendid, through the [supportless]{niralamba} yoga of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all [dharmas]{dharma}.
segments.note: Munidatta says the refrain makes joy firm (cp.31.m3). Akaṭa is ‘a wonder’. Compassion is conventional [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} (the mind of awakening in its relative form), which comes by way of the guru’s lineage. The ḍamaru is what makes the [unstruck]{anahata} sound, and unstruck knowledge awakens. So Āryadeva shines, supportless, in the yoga of apprehending no phenomenon.

flags.note: anāhataṃ hataṃ jñānaṃ vibudhyate looks corrupt: literally ‘unstruck, struck knowledge awakens’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gzhom du med pa'i sgra'i ye shes rnam par rtogs pa'o, ‘the knowledge of the unstruck sound is realized’, as if reading anāhataśabdajñānaṃ. I took hataṃ as a repetition of the end of anāhataṃ and translated ‘Unstruck knowledge awakens’; vibudhyate could also be passive, ‘is realized’.

Shastri prints a(ma)nāhataśabdaṃ. Read without the bracketed ma it is anāhataśabda, ‘unstruck sound’, which the next sentence and the Tibetan (gzhom du med pa'i sgra) confirm. I could not make sense of amanāhata. Munidatta (cp.31.m3) cites the drum as ḍamaruka, the usual Sanskrit form, where the song has ḍamaruli.

Shastri’s daṇḍa after āryadevapādāḥ cuts off the subject from rājate śobhate, and the honorific plural takes singular verbs. I read it as one sentence. nirālambena may qualify yogena (‘the supportless yoga’), as I took it, or stand alone as an adverb (‘supportlessly’). Either way it renders the song’s ṇirāse.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) differs in three places. (1) It glosses ya mtshan as rmad du byung ba'i snying rje, ‘wondrous compassion’, joining akaṭa to compassion, as its line 2a does. Munidatta’s Sanskrit (cp.31.m3) glosses akaṭa and karuṇā separately, which suits the draft’s ‘A wonder: …’. (2) It has bla ma'i drin las, ‘from the guru’s kindness’, for gurusampradāyāt. (3) It has rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug gis, ‘as lord of yogis’, where the Sanskrit has yogena, ‘through the yoga’.

segments.translit: dvitīyapadena viṣayasvarūpam āha— cānder ityādi| yathā astaṃ gate candramasi tasya candrikā tatraiva antarbhavati| cia iti| tathā cittarājo 'pi yadā acittatāṃ gacchati prabhāsvaraṃ viśati tadā tasya vikalpāvalī tatraiva līnā bhavatīti| tathā cāgamaḥ| astaṃ gate candramasīva nūnaṃ nīrendavaḥ saṃharaṇaṃ prayānti| cittaṃ hi tadvat sahaje [ni]līne naśyanty amī sarvavikalpadoṣāḥ||
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [sense objects]{visaya}. ‘In the moon…’ and so on: as, when the [moon]{moon} has set, its [moonlight]{moonlight} is absorbed into it right there. ‘[Mind]{citta}…’: so too, when the [king of mind]{king-of-mind} goes to [no-mind]{acittata} and enters [clear light]{prabhasvara}, its series of [conceptual thoughts]{vikalpa} dissolves right there. And so the [scripture]{agama}: ‘Just as, when the [moon]{moon} has set, the [moons in water]{udakacandra} surely go to their withdrawal, / so, when the [mind]{citta} has dissolved in the [innate]{sahaja}, / all these faults of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} perish.’
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 3 as a simile (cp.31.m4). As moonlight goes back into the moon when it sets, so the [king of mind]{king-of-mind} goes to no-mind and enters clear light, and its conceptual thoughts dissolve there. The setting is his: the song says only that moonlight shines in the moon. For 3b his paraphrase makes bikaraṇe the mind’s conceptual thoughts.

citations.quoted: astaṃ gate candramasīva nūnaṃ nīrendavaḥ saṃharaṇaṃ prayānti | cittaṃ hi tadvat sahaje [ni]līne naśyanty amī sarvavikalpadoṣāḥ ||
citations.work: not named: introduced only as ‘the scripture’ (āgama); not identified

flags.note: Song and commentary diverge here. Line 3a says only that moonlight shines in the moon (patibhāsaa, ‘appears, shines’). Munidatta (cp.31.m4) adds the setting, with the moonlight absorbed into the moon (antarbhavati), and builds a simile of dissolution on it (yathā … tathā): moon : king of mind :: moonlight : series of conceptual thoughts. The quoted verse adds moons in water. The draft line should stay as the song has it. The Tibetan line for 3a has yongs su shes, ‘fully knows’, for patibhāsaa; the comment does not take that up.

Bears on the song draft, 3b (bikaraṇe). Munidatta (cp.31.m4) does not gloss the word, but his paraphrase follows the line. The king of mind (cia) ‘enters’ clear light (viśati, echoing paisai). What dissolves ‘right there’ (tatraiva, for tahi) is its series of conceptual thoughts (vikalpāvalī), standing where the line has bikaraṇe. So he seems to take bikaraṇe as the mind’s changing states or thoughts, plural, rather than a single act of transformation. He has nothing for ṭali. The Tibetan comment cites rnam 'gyur (its word for bikaraṇe) where the Sanskrit cites cia.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the moonlight ‘set in’ the moon (nub par 'gyur) where the Sanskrit has it ‘absorbed’ (antarbhavati). It has the king of mind ‘dissolve into no-mind, clear light’ (sems med pa 'od gsal la thim) as one act, where the Sanskrit has two: it goes to no-mind and enters clear light. Its conceptual thoughts have no ‘series’ (āvalī). In the verse it has ‘however many moons in water set’ (chu yi zla ba ji snyed nub par 'gyur), and its last line lacks ‘faults’ (doṣa).

The verse is an upajāti, and Shastri’s restored [ni] in [ni]līne is needed for the metre. In its third line cittaṃ (nominative or accusative) stands with the locative nilīne. A locative absolute would want citte (same metre); the Tibetan makes the mind the subject (sems kyang lhan skyes la ni nub, ‘the mind too sets in the innate’). I translated ‘when the mind has dissolved in the innate’.

In viṣayasvarūpam āha I used the approved ‘sense objects’ for viṣaya. Here the word may mean ‘the object’ or ‘the subject matter’ of the verse. The Tibetan has yul gyi rang bzhin, ‘the nature of the object’. See questions.

segments.translit: tṛtīyapadena bhāvasya niraṃśatām āha— chāṛila ityādi| ataeva mayā siddhācāryeṇa bhayalajjādikaṃ lokasya vyavahāraḥ parityaktaḥ| guruvacanamārganirīkṣaṇena śūnyam iti|| bhāvaṃ nairātmyarū[paṃ] dṛṣṭaṃ|
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he states that [being]{bhava-being} is [partless]{niravayava}. ‘Having given up…’ and so on. That is why I, the [siddha]{siddha} master, have abandoned [fear]{bhaya}, [shame]{lajja} and the like, that is, [worldly custom]{lokacara}. By looking at the [path]{marga} of the [guru]{guru}'s word, ‘[emptiness]{sunyata}’: [being]{bhava-being} has been seen to have the form of [selflessness]{nairatmya}.
segments.note: Munidatta says couplet 4 shows that being is partless (cp.31.m5). The poet, as [siddha]{siddha} master (an accomplished adept), has given up fear, shame and the rest of worldly custom. Looking at the path of the guru’s word, he has seen being as empty, with the form of selflessness. Munidatta has shame where the song has disgust.

equations.en: being, seen to have the form of selflessness

flags.note: Munidatta (cp.31.m5) cites chāṛila (a past form, ‘gave up’) where the song has chāṛia (‘having given up’). The Tibetan comment cites spangs nas, ‘having abandoned’. I kept the draft’s wording for the cited line.

bhayalajjādikaṃ (neuter) stands beside vyavahāraḥ parityaktaḥ (masculine). I read the two in apposition: ‘fear, shame and the like, that is, worldly custom’. In the last sentence Shastri’s double daṇḍa after śūnyam iti splits what seems one sentence, and bhāvaṃ … dṛṣṭaṃ has an accusative where a passive wants a nominative. It may also be read ‘being has been seen as “empty”, having the form of selflessness’.

The Tibetan comment agrees on fear and shame ('jigs pa dang ngo tsha ba). Its line 4a, though, has srid pa'i skyug bro, ‘disgust at existence’, and no fear, as if reading bhava for bhaya. Its last sentence has ‘looking at’ (lta ba) where the Sanskrit has ‘seen’ (dṛṣṭa): dngos po ni bdag med pa'i gzugs la lta ba'o, ‘being: looking at the form of selflessness’.

Munidatta (cp.31.m5) leaves biāra (‘examination’, 4b) unglossed. His ‘looking at’ (nirīkṣaṇa) and ‘seen’ (dṛṣṭa) answer cāhante cāhante. He does not explain why this couplet shows that being is partless. The Tibetan agrees on the heading (dngos po cha shas med pa).

segments.translit: caturthapadenātmānuśaṃsām āha— āryadeva ityādi| āryadevapādena sadguruprasā[dā]t nairātmyadharmāmukhīkaraṇe sarvaṃ saṃsāradūṣaṇaṃ viphalīkṛtam iti|| 31||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states his [praise]{anusamsa} of himself. ‘[Āryadeva]{p-aryadeva}…’ and so on: by [Āryadeva]{p-aryadeva}, through the true [guru]{guru}'s [grace]{prasada}, in making the [dharma]{dharma} of [selflessness]{nairatmya} manifest, every fault of [saṃsāra]{samsara} has been made fruitless.
segments.note: Munidatta hears the poet praising himself (cp.31.m6). By the true guru’s grace Āryadeva made the dharma of selflessness manifest, and so made every fault of saṃsāra fruitless. ‘Made fruitless’ stands where 5a has bihariu, and ‘every fault of saṃsāra’ where it has ‘everything’. This supports the draft’s ‘done away with’ over the Tibetan line’s ‘examines’.

flags.note: Bears on the song draft, 5a (bihariu). Munidatta’s paraphrase (cp.31.m6) follows the line word for word. Āryadevapādena answers the instrumental ājadebem̐. sarvaṃ saṃsāradūṣaṇaṃ, ‘every fault of saṃsāra’, answers saala. viphalīkṛtam, ‘made fruitless’, answers bihariu. So he takes bihariu, like ṇibāriu in 5b, as a passive participle meaning something like ‘done away with, removed’. That supports the draft and tells against the Tibetan line’s kun la rnam par dpyod par byed, ‘examines everything’, and against ‘roamed’ (viharati). He does not quote the word.

dūṣaṇa can mean ‘fault, corruption’ or ‘refutation’. I translated ‘fault’. The Tibetan has both, 'khor ba'i skyon thams cad sun phyung nas, ‘having refuted all the faults of saṃsāra’, and then ‘made them fruitless’.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads bdag med pa'i chos thams cad mngon sum du mdzad nas, ‘having made all the dharmas of selflessness manifest’. It puts ‘all’ with the dharmas as well as with the faults, and treats āmukhīkaraṇa as an action completed before the faults are made fruitless.

proposals.definition: Shame (Sanskrit lajjā; Tibetan ngo tsha ba): concern for how one appears to others, which tantric conduct sets aside along with fear and disgust. Munidatta counts fear, shame and the like as the worldly custom the siddha master has abandoned, where song 31 names fear and disgust (cp.31.m5).
proposals.rationale: Munidatta puts lajjā where song 31 has ghiṇa, ‘disgust’ (cp.31.m5). The glossary’s bhaya and ghrna entries already mention shame, and the nirghrna entry says he explains ‘without disgust’ as free of faults such as shame, so the word recurs. I recall that tantric lists of eight bonds (aṣṭapāśa) name disgust, shame and fear together. That is from memory and needs checking before it goes into the definition.

questions: The glossary gives p-aryadeva only as ‘Āryadeva’, but Munidatta writes Āryadevapāda (cp.31.m1, cp.31.m3, cp.31.m6), and other siddha entries keep -pāda (Bhusukupāda, Cāṭilapāda). I used ‘Āryadeva’. Should ‘Āryadevapāda’ be added as a variant? The entry’s definition also describes the Āryadeva quoted at cp.01.m2 (a Guhyasamāja teacher). Here he is the poet of song 31, and the two may not be the same person, so the definition probably needs widening.

In cp.31.m4, viṣayasvarūpam āha (‘he states the true nature of …’) I used the approved ‘sense objects’ for viṣaya. ‘The object’ or ‘the subject matter’ may fit better (Tibetan yul gyi rang bzhin). Keep ‘sense objects’ here, or leave the word unlinked?

In cp.31.m3, anāhataṃ hataṃ jñānaṃ vibudhyate looks corrupt. I dropped hataṃ as a repetition and translated ‘Unstruck knowledge awakens’, with the Tibetan’s ‘knowledge of the unstruck sound is realized’ in a flag. Do you accept that, or should the translation show the text as it stands?

Equations: I recorded two kinds. Plain lexical glosses: akaṭa = ‘a wonder’, ḍamaruka = ‘what makes the unstruck sound’ (cp.31.m3). Lemma-plus-paraphrase glosses: apā (cp.31.m2) and cia (cp.31.m4) = ‘the king of mind’, śūnyam = ‘being, seen to have the form of selflessness’ (cp.31.m5). All of these become symbolic readings on approval. Drop any you do not want: the lexical ones are not symbolic, and cia is a simile’s second half rather than a flat equation.
In cp.31.m5 the hit list matched bhāvasya to bhava-abhava (‘being and nonbeing’). Munidatta’s word is bhāva alone, so I used bhava-being (‘being’). Please confirm.

I proposed a new entry, lajja (‘shame’), for Munidatta’s lajjā (cp.31.m5), which stands where the song has ‘disgust’. My memory that tantric lists of eight bonds (aṣṭapāśa) pair disgust, shame and fear needs checking.
The verse Munidatta quotes in cp.31.m4 as ‘the scripture’ (āgama), astaṃ gate candramasīva nūnaṃ…, is unidentified. Can you place it?

Three song-draft points are flagged but not changed. 1a (ho ṇa ṭhā): Munidatta’s gloss (cp.31.m2) supports ‘lost’ and also ‘entered’ (the Tibetan line). 3b (bikaraṇe): his paraphrase (cp.31.m4) takes it as the mind’s conceptual thoughts. 5a (bihariu): his ‘made fruitless’ (cp.31.m6) supports ‘done away with’ against the Tibetan ‘examines’. Separately, the Tibetan line 4a has srid pa, ‘existence’, where the Bengali has bhaya, ‘fear’ (bhava for bhaya?). That may deserve a witness note on the line.
